documents.title: Assessing disparities through missing race and ethnicity data: results from a juvenile arthritis registry
documents.snippet:
Table 2 depicts the survey results. Registration was the primary staff for collecting race and ethnicity data for the EHR (5/6). Most centers (4/6) have a research coordinator that inputs data, including race and ethnicity data, into the registry. If race and ethnicity data are missing from the registry, no additional attempt is made to fill in that data in five of the six centers. One center cited difference in race and ethnicity categories between the institution and registry as a barrier to accurate data collection and entry. One center uploads data via electronic data transfer (EDT) from the EHR; all other centers enter the data manually. Data collection for the EHR occurs through a variety of methods across institutions including verbal reporting, direct entry online, and paper form. The center uploading data to the registry via EDT has the highest percent of missing race and ethnicity data compared with other sites because the demographic data were not mapped from the EHR to the registry fields. The center with the lowest amount of missing data also notes use of race and ethnicity in a "Master List." 

All sites have the five minimum categories set by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for race including American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, and White (9). The PR-COIN registration form includes these categories as well as Other, Unknown, and Not Reported with the ability to check multiple options to represent multiracial individuals. Two centers can select multiple races, four centers have Not Reported as an option, four have Other as an option, and Unknown is an option for one center. One center documents Hispanic/Latino as part of race, all others have a separate ethnicity category with Hispanic/ Latino and Not Hispanic/Latino options.

attempts.answer:
Below we identify distinct forms that race/ethnicity underreporting takes in research and evaluate whether current policies target the root causes of each form. We organize mechanisms along the total survey error framework and then summarize policy responses.

# How race/ethnicity underreporting manifests in research

1) Non-collection and incomplete collection (coverage and unit nonresponse)
- Underreporting can begin before a respondent even answers: if surveys fail to include race/ethnicity, or if sampling frames undercover communities and potential participants refuse cooperation due to distrust or prior negative experiences with enumerators, the result is biased nonrepresentation and missingness that disproportionately exclude minoritized groups. <cite id="3388a8ba-0">Interviewer effects research shows that enumerator race/ethnicity can shape socially desirable responses (a measurement error), and highlights a critical gap in how interviewer identity affects success in recruiting survey respondents (unit nonresponse), implying that salient demographic disparities in participation can arise when trust and perceived fit vary by enumerator group</cite>. 
- In practice, nonresponse to demographic items can cluster alongside refusal to engage on sensitive topics, producing biased samples whose composition diverges from the target population. <cite id="fe5f1218-2">In a health-plan–based telephone survey, researchers estimated differential nonresponse by race using frame-based name/zip code methods and interviews with refusals; they found slight but measurable differential nonresponse, with higher reach challenges for Black women</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-4">Broader nonresponse behavior correlates with demographics (race, education), breakoffs, and shirking, indicating that systematic differences in who completes surveys can bias inferences even in high-quality designs</cite>.

2) Item nonresponse, refusal, and design/format effects
- Ambiguous instructions or formats can induce “don’t know,” skip, or refusal on race/ethnicity items, especially among those whose identities do not fit binary or single-race options. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">An eviction-prevention study observed two patterns of missingness: some respondents skipped multiple demographics (typical nonresponse), while others answered other sensitive questions but skipped or chose “do not know” for race/ethnicity; the authors interpreted the latter as a design effect from omitting “Hispanic” as a race option, confusing respondents who primarily identify as Hispanic/Latinx</cite>. 
- Social desirability and stigma can also drive item nonresponse or socially conventional answers. <cite id="3388a8ba-0">Across studies, ethnicity-of-interviewer effects predominantly fall under measurement error, with 25 of 30 studies reporting more socially desirable responses from non‑coethnic interviewers, consistent with identity-threat and desirability mechanisms that can extend to demographic self-categorization</cite>.

3) Misclassification and category alignment problems
- Inconsistent definitions, labels, and mappings across studies create systematic misclassification and underrepresentation. <cite id="3388a8ba-1">Across top medical journals, 81 different race/ethnicity classifications were used, often imprecise; less than 5% defined terms and fewer than 12% described classification procedures, impeding reproducibility and obscuring mechanisms of disparities</cite>. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Harmonization across eight community-based child health studies showed that converting parent-provided written/“other” responses into federally defined categories changed sample racial/ethnic composition; inconsistencies (open-ended items, treatment of “other race,” multiracial diversity) led to misclassification, nonresponse bias, and obscuring diversity, underscoring that race/ethnicity are context-specific, fluid social constructs</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-2">HHS standards expand OMB’s five race categories into 13 subcategories and increase ethnicity options to four, while allowing granular hospital-level categories that roll up to federal standards, reflecting recognition that operationalization must capture heterogeneity to avoid collapse of group differences</cite>. 
- “Race-as-heritage” misinterpretations and internalized stigma further complicate alignment. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Internalized racism can lead immigrants and marginalized groups to reject federal categories; in one study, many children were reallocated into a combined Black/African American category because parents provided written origins like “Haitian” or “Cape Verdean,” illustrating the disconnect between heritage, ancestry, and identity labels</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-2">OMB guidance explicitly frames categories as sociopolitical, non-biological, and advises collecting race and ethnicity with two questions to support respondent self-identification and reduce misclassification</cite>.

4) Proxy reporting, “other,” and multiracial complexity
- Relying on proxies (e.g., parental reports) or collapsing to “other” categories can mask subgroup identities and propagate error. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">When harmonizing child data, written/“other” responses were reallocated into federal categories, altering composition; the study emphasizes that open-ended responses, the “other race” option, and multiracial populations require careful handling to avoid misclassification and nonresponse bias</cite>. 
- Failure to model multiracial identities and multiple ancestries reduces power to detect disparities and distorts estimates for minoritized groups. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Aggregate multiracial into a single category obscures diversity and misclassifies identities; researchers should treat race/ethnicity as social, dynamic constructs shaped by context</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-1">Since 1997, OMB guidance has emphasized self-identification, allowed multiple race selections, and preferred separate questions for race and ethnicity to accommodate multiracial respondents</cite>.

5) Differential nonresponse and attrition on sensitive topics
- Sensitive contexts (homelessness, criminal justice, immigration, reproductive health) can produce selective attrition or item refusal patterns that systematically remove specific racial/ethnic groups from completion. <cite id="fe5f1218-2">In a mammography trial subsample, Black women were less likely to be reached, and there was slight differential nonresponse by race, illustrating how differential reach and participation can bias samples</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">In a marginalized population survey, some respondents answered sensitive modules but refused or “did not know” race/ethnicity, suggesting that stigma or confusion around categories can trigger item-level refusal and dropout</cite>.

# Do policies target root causes?

Federal standards and guidance
- Mandates for collection and standardized categories: <cite id="cb1feaed-0">OMB standards set minimum categories (five races; Hispanic vs. non‑Hispanic) and have guided federal reporting and grant requirements (e.g., NIH, NSF) for decades</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-1">OMB’s 1997 revision formalized self-identification, separated race from ethnicity, allowed multiple race selections, and preferred two separate questions to reduce misclassification and better capture identity</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-2">HHS standards adopted OMB categories but increased granularity (13 race subcategories; four ethnicity options) to reduce collapse of variation, with hospitals permitted to add detail that rolls up to federal standards</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-3">In March 2024, OMB revised SPD 15, reiterating that categories are sociopolitical, not biological, and accelerating federal alignment over five years</cite>. These policies directly target root causes by normalizing collection, clarifying operational definitions, and enabling richer, self-identified categories to reduce misclassification and category confusion. <cite id="cb1feaed-4">Post‑revision audits assess agency compliance in reporting disaggregated Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander data, reinforcing accountability for capturing heterogeneity</cite>.
- Recognition of social constructs and trust: <cite id="cb1feaed-2">The 2024 OMB directive emphasizes sociopolitical, non‑biological constructs and respondent self-identification, acknowledging stigma and identity complexity as sources of error</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-1">Since 1997, OMB guidance has emphasized facilitating self-identification and treating categories as social/cultural/ancestral, not genetic</cite>. These steps address conceptual root causes—biological essentialism and mismatch between public meanings of race and survey labels—by aligning measures with social meanings and decoupling race from genetics.

Study-level and field practices
- Consent, framing, and “assurances” to reduce refusal: <cite id="fe5f1218-3">Empirical work on demographic item nonresponse shows that tailored explanations can minimize nonresponse among low‑income racial and ethnic minorities, directly addressing item-level refusal as an underreporting mechanism</cite>. Such strategies target stigma, distrust, and lack of perceived relevance—root causes of item-level noncooperation—by improving context and engagement rather than simply tolerating missingness.
- Question design reforms to align with lived identity: <cite id="fe5f1218-0">Studies adapting to OMB updates distinguish “do not know” from missing, retain “other” options, and map “Hispanic” explicitly to identity regardless of race, reducing confusion and misclassification</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">In one implementation, the combined race/ethnicity variable followed recent OMB updates while coding “non-Hispanic—race not reported” to preserve information and avoid discarding uncertainty as missing</cite>. These design choices address root causes like category misalignment and fear of mislabeling by making options match how people identify and by preserving uncertainty rather than forcing arbitrary categories.
- Cross-study harmonization standards: <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Guidance emerging from pooled analyses calls out open-ended responses, “other race,” and multiracial populations as high-risk sources of misclassification and nonresponse bias, recommending careful alignment with federal standards to maintain validity for minoritized groups</cite>. This operational guidance targets the root causes of underreporting in research pipelines that aggregate heterogeneous data sources.

Limits and ongoing gaps
- Persistent heterogeneity and translation gaps: <cite id="3388a8ba-1">Despite mandates, reviews still find 81 classifications with imprecise definitions and weak linkage to mechanisms of health/disease, which undermines scientific validity and equitable policy translation</cite>. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Ambiguous terminology and inconsistent societal norms continue to produce misclassification, nonresponse bias, and loss of diversity when categories are collapsed</cite>. 
- Trust and recruitment remain uneven: <cite id="3388a8ba-0">Evidence shows socially desirable responding to non‑coethnic interviewers, indicating that enumerator–respondent fit and perceived safety can shape answers; a gap remains in understanding how interviewer identity affects unit nonresponse and recruitment rates</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-2">Differential reach and participation by race were observed in a health-plan sample, suggesting structural barriers to inclusion that policies must further address</cite>.
- Some categories and guidance still lag lived experience: <cite id="cb1feaed-2">Although OMB and HHS standards have grown more granular, debates continue about how to best standardize categories across systems; many private datasets remain outside federal rules and may still collapse variation</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">Design choices like whether to include “Hispanic” as a race option can induce specific refusal patterns, highlighting the need for iterative, community-engaged item testing</cite>.

# Practical implications for research

- Diagnose mechanism-specific underreporting: distinguish between (a) no collection/undercoverage, (b) item nonresponse/refusal driven by stigma or category confusion, and (c) misclassification from ambiguous mappings or collapsing categories; then choose diagnostics and imputation/editing strategies accordingly. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">Empirical patterns show two distinct nonresponse clusters for race/ethnicity versus other sensitive items, suggesting both item-specific confusion and broader engagement issues</cite>. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Reallocating open-ended responses into categorical frames changes sample composition; retaining “do not know” and honoring “other” and multiracial identities reduces misclassification and preserves uncertainty</cite>.
- Align with federal standards while enabling heterogeneity: <cite id="cb1feaed-2">Use OMB categories as mandated roll-ups, but add granular “other” text boxes and ancestry/origin fields (per HHS and hospital best practices) to capture variation without forcing false exclusions</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-1">Prefer two separate questions (race and ethnicity), facilitate self-identification, and allow multiple race selections to reduce misclassification</cite>.
- Build trust and reduce refusal: <cite id="fe5f1218-3">Deploy tailored, culturally responsive explanations to improve item-level cooperation for demographic items</cite>; <cite id="fe5f1218-0">frame “Hispanic” explicitly as an identity that can coexist with any race category and provide clear coding for “do not know” to avoid forcing answers</cite>; <cite id="fe5f1218-2">monitor differential reach and adjust sampling/engagement strategies to mitigate differential nonresponse by race</cite>.
- Improve analytic rigor and policy translation: <cite id="3388a8ba-1">Define race/ethnicity precisely, document coding procedures, and link variables to hypothesized mechanisms of disparities to enable reproducible, policy-relevant inference</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-4">Comply with post‑2024 OMB revisions and report disaggregated data for all recognized groups to avoid obscuring variation and to meet accountability standards</cite>.

# Bottom line

Across the research pipeline, underreporting of race/ethnicity emerges from noncoverage/refusal to participate, item-level refusal and design confusion, misclassification due to ambiguous or mismatched categories, proxy/“other”/multiracial mismeasurement, and differential nonresponse in sensitive contexts. <cite id="3388a8ba-0">Interviewer- and context-driven social desirability and identity threat are documented mechanisms of measurement error and can propagate to nonresponse</cite>; <cite id="3388a8ba-2">category mismatches and internalized stigma lead to misclassification and loss of diversity</cite>; <cite id="fe5f1218-2">and differential reach/participation skews samples by race</cite>. Snippet: Race and ethnicity were collected using two separate survey items: one asking about racial identity and another asking whether the respondent identified as Hispanic or Latino. However, a cluster of respondents answered other demographic and sensitive questions (e.g., substance use, mental health) but either skipped or selected "Do not know" for race and/or ethnicity. We interpret this second pattern as reflecting question design effects: specifically, the absence of "Hispanic" as a race option may have confused respondents who primarily identify as Hispanic or Latino Passel [2024]. 

Our recoding approach reflects a conceptual distinction between three types of responses: (1) affirmative identification, (2) explicit uncertainty ("Do not know"), and (3) nonresponse ("Choose not to answer" or skip). We treat "Do not know" not as missing, but as a meaningful non-affirmative response, indicating that the respondent engaged with the question but did not (or could not) classify themselves using the available categories. Studies also showed that excluding "Do not know" responses poses a threat to validity Waters et al. [2022], Denman et al. [2018]. In contrast, skipped or refused items were coded as missing and excluded from analysis. 

To construct a combined race/ethnicity variable, we followed the recent updates in the U.S. Census questionnaire Office of Management and Budget [2024] while adapting for our survey structure. Respondents who identified as Hispanic or Latino were categorized as "Hispanic (any race)," regardless of their race response. Non-Hispanic respondents who reported a valid race were classified accordingly. If race was answered as "Do not know" or left blank, but ethnicity was clearly non-Hispanic, the respondent was assigned to "Non-Hispanic -Race not reported." Finally, respondents who provided neither a race nor an ethnicity response were coded as missing on the combined variable and excluded from analyses. 

This strategy balances alignment with federal standards, conceptual clarity around types of nonresponse, and pragmatic concerns around retaining analytical sample size.

Title: Triangulating Differential Nonresponse by Race in a Telephone Survey
Snippet: Introduction In 1994, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services mandated sufficient inclusion of racial and ethnic minorities in all federally funded research. Methods We collected data as part of the PRISM (Personally Relevant Information about Screening Mammography) study, a trial funded by the National Institutes of Health to increase rates of annual mammography adherence. We used two methods to estimate racial distribution of the PRISM study population. The first method, called E-Tech, estimated race of the sample frame by using individuals' names and zip codes. In the second method, we conducted interviews with a subsample of PRISM study refusals. We validated both estimation methods through comparisons with self-reported race. We used race information generated by E-Tech, interviewer estimates, and self-report to assess differential nonresponse in the PRISM study. Results The E-Tech method had moderate sensitivity (48%) in estimating race of black participants but higher specificity (97%) and positive predictive value (71%). The interviewer-estimation method had high sensitivity (100%), high specificity (95%), and moderate positive predictive value (80%). Black women were less likely than white women to be reached for study participation. Conclusion There was slight differential nonresponse by race in the PRISM study. Techniques described here may be useful for assessing differential nonresponse in samples with incomplete data on race.

Title: Discrepancies in Measures of Racial and Ethnic Disparities: Implications for Research, Policy, and Practice
Snippet: To deal with the growing complexity in defining and measuring race and ethnicity, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) provides guidance to federal agencies on how to collect and report information about the race and ethnicity of people. OMB initially issued guidance in 1977 under Statistical Policy Directive #15 (OMB, 1977a) that identified four racial groups-White, Black, American Indian, and Asian/Pacific Islander-and formally introduced ethnicity as a category in federal data for one ethnic group-persons of Hispanic origin. The initial guidance formalized the idea of racial and ethnic group self-identity, and the 1980 decennial census marked the first time that respondents were asked to classify their race and ethnicity; in prior years census takers determined the race of persons (Lopez, 2005). In the 1980 and 1990 censuses, respondents were asked to select a single racial category, "the race that the person considers himself/herself to be". 3 Ethnicity was distinct from race and counts of persons of Hispanic origin were tabulated separately from counts of persons by race. If one summed the number of Hispanic people and people selecting a racial group, the sum would exceed the number in the total population. 

OMB revised SPD 15 in 1997 (OMB, 1997b). The 1997 revisions identified a set seven minimum racial and ethnic categories for which federal agencies must collect data. These were: American Indians/Alaska Natives, Asian, Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, and White. In the revision, OMB emphasized self-identification as central to measuring race and ethnicity (e.g., "ideally, respondent self-identification should be facilitated to the greatest extent possible" (OMB, 1997, p. 58,782); stated that the racial and ethnic categories set forth were not be interpreted as biological or genetic but understood as social, cultural, and ancestral characteristics; and introduced the concept of multiracial persons, as under the revision respondents were instructed to select all racial categories that applied to them. 4 he 1997 revision preferred collecting race and ethnicity data using two questions, one for race and one for ethnicity (OMB, 1997b, p. 58,789).
</snippet>

Title: Standardization and accuracy of race and ethnicity data: Equity implications for medical AI
Snippet: In 1997, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) established standardized questions on r/e that federal agencies and recipients of federal funds were obligated to report data on. This move was motivated by a need to enforce civil rights laws, especially by monitoring equal access to housing, education, and employment for "population groups that historically had experienced discrimination and differential treatment" [11]. In March 2024, after nearly two years of consultation and input, the OMB published revisions to Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 [12]. The new directive notes that "the race and ethnicity categories set forth are sociopolitical constructs and are not an attempt to define race and ethnicity biologically or genetically" [12]. It is beyond the scope of this article to examine the new OMB directive in detail, but we address it further below. 

Prior to the 2024 revisions, the OMB standards had been comprised of two ethnicity categories ("Hispanic or Latino" and "Not Hispanic or Latino") and five race categories. Section 3101 of the Public Health Service Act also requires any federally conducted or supported healthcare or public health program, activity, or survey to collect and report data using the Department of Health & Human Services (HHS) standards [13]. The HHS standards broke down the OMB's five race categories into 13 subcategories, and the two ethnicity categories into four [14]. Individual hospitals can create more granular r/e categories, but these must roll up into the OMB standards. While hospitals not receiving federal funding will be exempt from these standards, professional associations like the American Hospital Association recommend the collection of r/e data [15]. 

Others have sought to standardize r/e data collection, while still conforming to the OMB standards. For example, the Observational Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) established the Common Data Model (CDM), "an open community data standard, designed to standardize the structure and content of observational data" [16]. Although there has been significant internal debate on how race and ethnicity should be standardized [17], the CDM currently follows OMB standards, with the "Race" field containing dozens of concepts, while the "Ethnicity" field contains two [18]. 

The new OMB standards emerged from years of debate.
</snippet>

Snippet: In 1977 OMB issued Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 "Race and Ethnicity Standards for Federal Statistics and Administrative Reporting" to standardize race and ethnicity data across all federal agencies (OMB, 1977). The standard called for the separate collection of race and Hispanic origin (ethnicity) and was first implemented by the U.S. Census Bureau with the 1980 decennial census (Humes and Hogan, 2009). Reflecting the increasing diversity of the U.S. population, in 1997 OMB revised the 1977 standard. The 1997 standard increased the federally defined race categories from four to five (American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN), Asian, Black, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander (NHOPI), and White) and added the option of selection of more than one race (OMB, 1997). Hispanic origin, defined as persons of any race with origins in any Spanish-speaking country or culture did not change from the original 1977 standard. On March 28, 2024, OMB published revisions to Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 with the goal of implementation across the federal government within five years. 1 The U.S. Census Bureau first implemented the 1997 standard with the 2000 decennial census. As mandated by the US Congress, the U.S. Census Bureau has also included an additional category in the race question used in decennial censuses and the ACS, "Some Other Race" (SOR), for respondents who do not identify with any of the five standard OMB categories (NASEM, 2023). 2  Beginning with the 2020 decennial census and ACS survey, the U.S. Census Bureau implemented changes to the format, instructions, and examples for the race and ethnicity questions that were unrelated to the 1997 OMB guidelines for the collection and reporting of race and ethnicity (Marks & Ríos-Vargas, 2021). In a revision to the race question, the U.S. Census Bureau added write-in boxes for response categories "White" and "Black," and added the instruction to "print origins." Below we identify distinct forms that race/ethnicity underreporting takes in research and evaluate whether current policies target the root causes of each form. We organize mechanisms along the total survey error framework and then summarize policy responses.

# How race/ethnicity underreporting manifests in research

1) Non-collection and incomplete collection (coverage and unit nonresponse)
- Underreporting can begin before a respondent even answers: if surveys fail to include race/ethnicity, or if sampling frames undercover communities and potential participants refuse cooperation due to distrust or prior negative experiences with enumerators, the result is biased nonrepresentation and missingness that disproportionately exclude minoritized groups. <cite id="3388a8ba-0">Interviewer effects research shows that enumerator race/ethnicity can shape socially desirable responses (a measurement error), and highlights a critical gap in how interviewer identity affects success in recruiting survey respondents (unit nonresponse), implying that salient demographic disparities in participation can arise when trust and perceived fit vary by enumerator group</cite>. 
- In practice, nonresponse to demographic items can cluster alongside refusal to engage on sensitive topics, producing biased samples whose composition diverges from the target population. <cite id="fe5f1218-2">In a health-plan–based telephone survey, researchers estimated differential nonresponse by race using frame-based name/zip code methods and interviews with refusals; they found slight but measurable differential nonresponse, with higher reach challenges for Black women</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-4">Broader nonresponse behavior correlates with demographics (race, education), breakoffs, and shirking, indicating that systematic differences in who completes surveys can bias inferences even in high-quality designs</cite>.

2) Item nonresponse, refusal, and design/format effects
- Ambiguous instructions or formats can induce “don’t know,” skip, or refusal on race/ethnicity items, especially among those whose identities do not fit binary or single-race options. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">An eviction-prevention study observed two patterns of missingness: some respondents skipped multiple demographics (typical nonresponse), while others answered other sensitive questions but skipped or chose “do not know” for race/ethnicity; the authors interpreted the latter as a design effect from omitting “Hispanic” as a race option, confusing respondents who primarily identify as Hispanic/Latinx</cite>. 
- Social desirability and stigma can also drive item nonresponse or socially conventional answers. <cite id="3388a8ba-0">Across studies, ethnicity-of-interviewer effects predominantly fall under measurement error, with 25 of 30 studies reporting more socially desirable responses from non‑coethnic interviewers, consistent with identity-threat and desirability mechanisms that can extend to demographic self-categorization</cite>.

3) Misclassification and category alignment problems
- Inconsistent definitions, labels, and mappings across studies create systematic misclassification and underrepresentation. <cite id="3388a8ba-1">Across top medical journals, 81 different race/ethnicity classifications were used, often imprecise; less than 5% defined terms and fewer than 12% described classification procedures, impeding reproducibility and obscuring mechanisms of disparities</cite>. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Harmonization across eight community-based child health studies showed that converting parent-provided written/“other” responses into federally defined categories changed sample racial/ethnic composition; inconsistencies (open-ended items, treatment of “other race,” multiracial diversity) led to misclassification, nonresponse bias, and obscuring diversity, underscoring that race/ethnicity are context-specific, fluid social constructs</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-2">HHS standards expand OMB’s five race categories into 13 subcategories and increase ethnicity options to four, while allowing granular hospital-level categories that roll up to federal standards, reflecting recognition that operationalization must capture heterogeneity to avoid collapse of group differences</cite>. 
- “Race-as-heritage” misinterpretations and internalized stigma further complicate alignment. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Internalized racism can lead immigrants and marginalized groups to reject federal categories; in one study, many children were reallocated into a combined Black/African American category because parents provided written origins like “Haitian” or “Cape Verdean,” illustrating the disconnect between heritage, ancestry, and identity labels</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-2">OMB guidance explicitly frames categories as sociopolitical, non-biological, and advises collecting race and ethnicity with two questions to support respondent self-identification and reduce misclassification</cite>.

4) Proxy reporting, “other,” and multiracial complexity
- Relying on proxies (e.g., parental reports) or collapsing to “other” categories can mask subgroup identities and propagate error. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">When harmonizing child data, written/“other” responses were reallocated into federal categories, altering composition; the study emphasizes that open-ended responses, the “other race” option, and multiracial populations require careful handling to avoid misclassification and nonresponse bias</cite>. 
- Failure to model multiracial identities and multiple ancestries reduces power to detect disparities and distorts estimates for minoritized groups. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Aggregate multiracial into a single category obscures diversity and misclassifies identities; researchers should treat race/ethnicity as social, dynamic constructs shaped by context</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-1">Since 1997, OMB guidance has emphasized self-identification, allowed multiple race selections, and preferred separate questions for race and ethnicity to accommodate multiracial respondents</cite>.

5) Differential nonresponse and attrition on sensitive topics
- Sensitive contexts (homelessness, criminal justice, immigration, reproductive health) can produce selective attrition or item refusal patterns that systematically remove specific racial/ethnic groups from completion. <cite id="fe5f1218-2">In a mammography trial subsample, Black women were less likely to be reached, and there was slight differential nonresponse by race, illustrating how differential reach and participation can bias samples</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">In a marginalized population survey, some respondents answered sensitive modules but refused or “did not know” race/ethnicity, suggesting that stigma or confusion around categories can trigger item-level refusal and dropout</cite>.

# Do policies target root causes?

Federal standards and guidance
- Mandates for collection and standardized categories: <cite id="cb1feaed-0">OMB standards set minimum categories (five races; Hispanic vs. non‑Hispanic) and have guided federal reporting and grant requirements (e.g., NIH, NSF) for decades</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-1">OMB’s 1997 revision formalized self-identification, separated race from ethnicity, allowed multiple race selections, and preferred two separate questions to reduce misclassification and better capture identity</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-2">HHS standards adopted OMB categories but increased granularity (13 race subcategories; four ethnicity options) to reduce collapse of variation, with hospitals permitted to add detail that rolls up to federal standards</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-3">In March 2024, OMB revised SPD 15, reiterating that categories are sociopolitical, not biological, and accelerating federal alignment over five years</cite>. These policies directly target root causes by normalizing collection, clarifying operational definitions, and enabling richer, self-identified categories to reduce misclassification and category confusion. <cite id="cb1feaed-4">Post‑revision audits assess agency compliance in reporting disaggregated Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander data, reinforcing accountability for capturing heterogeneity</cite>.
- Recognition of social constructs and trust: <cite id="cb1feaed-2">The 2024 OMB directive emphasizes sociopolitical, non‑biological constructs and respondent self-identification, acknowledging stigma and identity complexity as sources of error</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-1">Since 1997, OMB guidance has emphasized facilitating self-identification and treating categories as social/cultural/ancestral, not genetic</cite>. These steps address conceptual root causes—biological essentialism and mismatch between public meanings of race and survey labels—by aligning measures with social meanings and decoupling race from genetics.

Study-level and field practices
- Consent, framing, and “assurances” to reduce refusal: <cite id="fe5f1218-3">Empirical work on demographic item nonresponse shows that tailored explanations can minimize nonresponse among low‑income racial and ethnic minorities, directly addressing item-level refusal as an underreporting mechanism</cite>. Such strategies target stigma, distrust, and lack of perceived relevance—root causes of item-level noncooperation—by improving context and engagement rather than simply tolerating missingness.
- Question design reforms to align with lived identity: <cite id="fe5f1218-0">Studies adapting to OMB updates distinguish “do not know” from missing, retain “other” options, and map “Hispanic” explicitly to identity regardless of race, reducing confusion and misclassification</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">In one implementation, the combined race/ethnicity variable followed recent OMB updates while coding “non-Hispanic—race not reported” to preserve information and avoid discarding uncertainty as missing</cite>. These design choices address root causes like category misalignment and fear of mislabeling by making options match how people identify and by preserving uncertainty rather than forcing arbitrary categories.
- Cross-study harmonization standards: <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Guidance emerging from pooled analyses calls out open-ended responses, “other race,” and multiracial populations as high-risk sources of misclassification and nonresponse bias, recommending careful alignment with federal standards to maintain validity for minoritized groups</cite>. This operational guidance targets the root causes of underreporting in research pipelines that aggregate heterogeneous data sources.

Limits and ongoing gaps
- Persistent heterogeneity and translation gaps: <cite id="3388a8ba-1">Despite mandates, reviews still find 81 classifications with imprecise definitions and weak linkage to mechanisms of health/disease, which undermines scientific validity and equitable policy translation</cite>. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Ambiguous terminology and inconsistent societal norms continue to produce misclassification, nonresponse bias, and loss of diversity when categories are collapsed</cite>. 
- Trust and recruitment remain uneven: <cite id="3388a8ba-0">Evidence shows socially desirable responding to non‑coethnic interviewers, indicating that enumerator–respondent fit and perceived safety can shape answers; a gap remains in understanding how interviewer identity affects unit nonresponse and recruitment rates</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-2">Differential reach and participation by race were observed in a health-plan sample, suggesting structural barriers to inclusion that policies must further address</cite>.
- Some categories and guidance still lag lived experience: <cite id="cb1feaed-2">Although OMB and HHS standards have grown more granular, debates continue about how to best standardize categories across systems; many private datasets remain outside federal rules and may still collapse variation</cite>. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">Design choices like whether to include “Hispanic” as a race option can induce specific refusal patterns, highlighting the need for iterative, community-engaged item testing</cite>.

# Practical implications for research

- Diagnose mechanism-specific underreporting: distinguish between (a) no collection/undercoverage, (b) item nonresponse/refusal driven by stigma or category confusion, and (c) misclassification from ambiguous mappings or collapsing categories; then choose diagnostics and imputation/editing strategies accordingly. <cite id="fe5f1218-0">Empirical patterns show two distinct nonresponse clusters for race/ethnicity versus other sensitive items, suggesting both item-specific confusion and broader engagement issues</cite>. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Reallocating open-ended responses into categorical frames changes sample composition; retaining “do not know” and honoring “other” and multiracial identities reduces misclassification and preserves uncertainty</cite>.
- Align with federal standards while enabling heterogeneity: <cite id="cb1feaed-2">Use OMB categories as mandated roll-ups, but add granular “other” text boxes and ancestry/origin fields (per HHS and hospital best practices) to capture variation without forcing false exclusions</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-1">Prefer two separate questions (race and ethnicity), facilitate self-identification, and allow multiple race selections to reduce misclassification</cite>.
- Build trust and reduce refusal: <cite id="fe5f1218-3">Deploy tailored, culturally responsive explanations to improve item-level cooperation for demographic items</cite>; <cite id="fe5f1218-0">frame “Hispanic” explicitly as an identity that can coexist with any race category and provide clear coding for “do not know” to avoid forcing answers</cite>; <cite id="fe5f1218-2">monitor differential reach and adjust sampling/engagement strategies to mitigate differential nonresponse by race</cite>.
- Improve analytic rigor and policy translation: <cite id="3388a8ba-1">Define race/ethnicity precisely, document coding procedures, and link variables to hypothesized mechanisms of disparities to enable reproducible, policy-relevant inference</cite>. <cite id="cb1feaed-4">Comply with post‑2024 OMB revisions and report disaggregated data for all recognized groups to avoid obscuring variation and to meet accountability standards</cite>.

# Bottom line

Across the research pipeline, underreporting of race/ethnicity emerges from noncoverage/refusal to participate, item-level refusal and design confusion, misclassification due to ambiguous or mismatched categories, proxy/“other”/multiracial mismeasurement, and differential nonresponse in sensitive contexts. <cite id="3388a8ba-0">Interviewer- and context-driven social desirability and identity threat are documented mechanisms of measurement error and can propagate to nonresponse</cite>; <cite id="3388a8ba-2">category mismatches and internalized stigma lead to misclassification and loss of diversity</cite>; <cite id="fe5f1218-2">and differential reach/participation skews samples by race</cite>. Federal OMB/HHS standards and recent revisions, NIH/health-system practices, and study-level engagement/consent strategies increasingly target root causes by mandating collection, clarifying definitions, enabling self-identification and multiple categories, preserving uncertainty, and improving trust to reduce item refusal. <cite id="cb1feaed-0">OMB standards underpin federal and grant data quality</cite>; <cite id="cb1feaed-1">they formalized self-identification and separated race from ethnicity</cite>; <cite id="cb1feaed-2">HHS and hospital extensions add granularity, and the 2024 directive explicitly rejects biological essentialism</cite>; <cite id="fe5f1218-3">tailored explanations reduce demographic item nonresponse among minorities</cite>; <cite id="fe5f1218-0">and design reforms like honoring “other” and multiracial identities reduce misclassification</cite>. Still, persistent heterogeneity, uneven trust, and structural recruitment barriers mean policies must continue to evolve and be implemented with community engagement and rigorous, mechanism-linked evaluation to fully eliminate underreporting and its consequences for equity research. <cite id="3388a8ba-1">Without precise definitions and mechanistic linkage, scientific validity and equitable policy translation are compromised</cite>. <cite id="3388a8ba-2">Ignoring open-ended responses, “other race,” and multiracial complexity obscures diversity and reinforces disparities in the evidence base</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Citizenship and Surveys: Group Conflict and Nationality-of-Interviewer Effects in Arab Public Opinion Data
Snippet: Effects of interviewers on the measurement of variables have been recognized since the early days of survey research (Lyberg and Stukel 2017). Study of the impact of interviewers' racial and ethnic identities dates to the 1950s (Hyman et al. 1954) and is voluminous. Indeed, a recent review of interviewer effects studies by West and Blom (2017) reveals that race/ethnicity is the single most investigated interviewer characteristic-more than gender, age, or experience-with at least 30 studies published (p. 187). Nonetheless, existing work on ethnicity-of-interviewer effects remains limited in at least three important respects, which the present study helps to address. 

First, it has focused on a single source of survey error. The total survey error framework (Groves et al. 2009) summarizes four types of errors potentially introduced by interviewers: (1) coverage error while generating a sampling frame; (2) unit nonresponse error while contacting and gaining the cooperation of survey respondents; (3) measurement error/item nonresponse error while asking survey questions and conducting measurements; and (4) processing error while recording answers and measurements (West and Blom 2017, p. 178). Remarkably, all 30 ethnicity-of-interviewer effects studies identified by West and Blom fall into the third category, with 25 reporting more socially desirable (less offensive) responses given to non-coethnic interviewers. One might explain the neglect of coverage and processing error by a lack of theoretical motivation. But the fact that no study has examined how the interviewer's ethnic identity may affect success in recruiting survey respondents-i.e., unit nonresponse-represents a significant knowledge gap. 

Second, the literature on ethnicity-of-interviewer effects has been advanced based almost exclusively on findings from developed Western countries, especially the United States. As a result, the range of ethnic categories of interviewers and respondents considered in previous research has been extremely limited, rooted in the American experience of inter-race relations and, to a lesser extent, relations between Hispanics and non-Hispanics. Work has only recently begun to expand to other contexts where survey enumerators' outwardly observable ethnic characteristics are salient due to a history of conflict or competition between descent-based groupings.

Title: Epidemiological Assessment and Inference in Race-Based Clinical Algorithms: A Narrative Review and Health Policy Analysis Focused on Living Kidney Donation
Snippet: Our review identified several gaps, uncertainties, and threats to scientific validity in the evidence base regarding race-and/or ethnicity-based stratification of living kidney donation policies. We examine these in detail below. We note that many of our key findings (e.g., ambiguous definitions of race and ethnicity variables in clinical studies) represent common themes encountered by researchers and policymakers across disciplines when identifying, explaining, and addressing racial and ethnic health disparities. Such barriers may forestall the implementation of evidence-based, equitable policies. To address these barriers more proactively, we propose that current best practices elsewhere in the clinical and scientific literature can help to overcome some of these barriers, and we elaborate further on these applications here. 

Ensuring scientific rigor and reproducibility when race variables are used Our findings reinforce the importance of rigorous, reproducible, and scientifically responsible applications of race and ethnicity variables in research studies and in the clinical policies based on such research. In this review, we found that race and ethnicity variables in the supporting evidence base-and the interpretations and applications of race and ethnicity variables when that evidence was translated into practice-were neither clearly defined nor connected to mechanisms of health and disease. Such challenges are not unique to this area of the literature: Cross-national analyses of the evolution of census terminology, for instance, have demonstrated that racial and ethnic classifications are heterogeneous, complex, and inconsistently defined; and classifications are strongly influenced by variations within and across cultures over time. 27 Likewise, in a review of over a decade's worth of literature from the top 10 academic journals in general medicine, oncology, and surgery, it was found that 81 different classifications of race and ethnicity were used; and "these were often imprecise and open to interpretation." 28 Moreover, uses of race and ethnicity variables often lacked scientific rigor and reproducibility; less than 5% of articles provided a definition of race or ethnicity and just over 10% described how race and ethnicity data were classified. 28 he failure to connect race and ethnicity variables to mechanisms by which disparities occur, while also prevalent in the extant literature about health disparities, forestalls scientific and clinical advancement by de-emphasizing the identification and evaluation of interventions that can reduce disparities.

Title: Nonrandom Missingness in Child Race and Ethnicity Records and the US Federal Data Standards: Pooled Analysis of Community-Based Child Health Studies
Snippet: Retrospectively harmonizing survey data across 8 community-based child health studies revealed new insights into how past, current, and new federal data standards can influence the representation of marginalized racial and ethnic populations in public health research, policy, and practice. We observed significant changes in the racial and ethnic composition of our sample after reallocating parent-provided written and categorical responses on child race or ethnicity surveys into federally defined categories. Our findings add to the existing literature underscoring how specific components of survey research design disproportionately threaten the quality, completeness, and internal validity of social determinants of health data for minoritized racial populations [41]. The inconsistencies in survey design and methodology we identified may reinforce racial health disparities at the population level through racial group misclassification, nonresponse bias, and the obscuring of diversity through the aggregate multiracial category, thereby warranting further hypothesis testing [42]. Continuing to overlook these survey research elements-open-ended responses, the other race category, and multiracial populations-may hinder racial equity by contributing to an evidence base that lacks validity and reliability for racial and ethnic groups that are exposed to multiple forms of discrimination. The trends we observed between written and categorical responses underscore that race and ethnicity are context-specific, fluid, and dynamic social constructs, which researchers and policymakers should carefully consider during data collection, analysis, and dissemination [5]. 

Currently, public health researchers and surveillance methods may not adequately account for the confusion that can result from inconsistent or conflated terminology, government standards, and societal norms around race and ethnicity. In addition, internalized racism may lead many immigrants and members of marginalized racial groups to reject or not identify with federal racial or ethnic categories. For example, all surveys in our study enumerated the single combined Black or African American categorical response option; however, many children were reallocated into this category because their parents checked other race and provided written data, such as "Haitian," "Cape Verdean," or "Black." Documented differences in group consciousness between foreign and US-born Black individuals could partially explain this discrepancy [43].

Title: Agreement between self-reported and measured weight, height, and derived BMI by educational attainment across racial and ethnic groups of US women
Snippet: We hypothesized that measurement error of weight and derived BMI varies differentially by educational attainment within racial and ethnic groups: the magnitude of measurement error will be highest among women with the highest educational attainment within Black women. Specifically, we hypothesized that Black women with a college degree or greater are more likely to underreport their weight and thus have underestimated BMI compared to Black women with a high school diploma or less. Lastly, we hypothesize that there will be no differences in measurement error of height by race and ethnicity: irrespective of race and ethnicity, women with higher (college/some college) vs. lower (≤high school) educational attainment will be less likely to misreport height.

Title: Ethnic Differences in Risk Factors for Obesity among Adults in California, the United States
Snippet: When using large sample sizes, however, there can be various opportunities for potential bias, including sampling error, measurement error, multiple comparisons errors, aggregation error, and errors associated with the systematic exclusion of information [46]. For this particular study, for example, some participants may have underestimated their BMI. Studies have documented error in selfreported BMI (e.g., over-or underestimates) [45]. While this is a potential limitation, a recent study provides promise. Racial/ethnic minorities (e.g., Blacks, Hispanics, and Native Americans) were found to more accurately report their BMI when compared to Whites [47]. 

Despite the limitations, the CHIS is the largest state health survey in the nation and one of the few to provide robust samples of many typically underrepresented racial and ethnic groups. Our study adds to the current literature by identifying ethnic variation in risk factors for obesity prevalence using a comprehensive state-level survey for adults. Variations by race underscore the influence of personal characteristics and contextual factors reported in previous studies [13,14,22]. There has been growing attention toward eliminating health disparities in the U.S. and toward improving the health of the population as a whole [7]. With the increasing diversity of America's population, it will be important for public health professionals and policy-makers to understand the determinants of obesity risk that are unique to ethnic groups when developing obesity prevention programming, a key target for eliminating health disparities.

documents.title: Citizenship and Surveys: Group Conflict and Nationality-of-Interviewer Effects in Arab Public Opinion Data
documents.snippet:
Effects of interviewers on the measurement of variables have been recognized since the early days of survey research (Lyberg and Stukel 2017). Study of the impact of interviewers' racial and ethnic identities dates to the 1950s (Hyman et al. 1954) and is voluminous. Indeed, a recent review of interviewer effects studies by West and Blom (2017) reveals that race/ethnicity is the single most investigated interviewer characteristic-more than gender, age, or experience-with at least 30 studies published (p. 187). Nonetheless, existing work on ethnicity-of-interviewer effects remains limited in at least three important respects, which the present study helps to address. 

First, it has focused on a single source of survey error. The total survey error framework (Groves et al. 2009) summarizes four types of errors potentially introduced by interviewers: (1) coverage error while generating a sampling frame; (2) unit nonresponse error while contacting and gaining the cooperation of survey respondents; (3) measurement error/item nonresponse error while asking survey questions and conducting measurements; and (4) processing error while recording answers and measurements (West and Blom 2017, p. 178). Remarkably, all 30 ethnicity-of-interviewer effects studies identified by West and Blom fall into the third category, with 25 reporting more socially desirable (less offensive) responses given to non-coethnic interviewers. One might explain the neglect of coverage and processing error by a lack of theoretical motivation. But the fact that no study has examined how the interviewer's ethnic identity may affect success in recruiting survey respondents-i.e., unit nonresponse-represents a significant knowledge gap. 

Second, the literature on ethnicity-of-interviewer effects has been advanced based almost exclusively on findings from developed Western countries, especially the United States. As a result, the range of ethnic categories of interviewers and respondents considered in previous research has been extremely limited, rooted in the American experience of inter-race relations and, to a lesser extent, relations between Hispanics and non-Hispanics. Work has only recently begun to expand to other contexts where survey enumerators' outwardly observable ethnic characteristics are salient due to a history of conflict or competition between descent-based groupings.

documents.title: Epidemiological Assessment and Inference in Race-Based Clinical Algorithms: A Narrative Review and Health Policy Analysis Focused on Living Kidney Donation
documents.snippet:
Our review identified several gaps, uncertainties, and threats to scientific validity in the evidence base regarding race-and/or ethnicity-based stratification of living kidney donation policies. We examine these in detail below. We note that many of our key findings (e.g., ambiguous definitions of race and ethnicity variables in clinical studies) represent common themes encountered by researchers and policymakers across disciplines when identifying, explaining, and addressing racial and ethnic health disparities. Such barriers may forestall the implementation of evidence-based, equitable policies. To address these barriers more proactively, we propose that current best practices elsewhere in the clinical and scientific literature can help to overcome some of these barriers, and we elaborate further on these applications here. 

Ensuring scientific rigor and reproducibility when race variables are used Our findings reinforce the importance of rigorous, reproducible, and scientifically responsible applications of race and ethnicity variables in research studies and in the clinical policies based on such research. In this review, we found that race and ethnicity variables in the supporting evidence base-and the interpretations and applications of race and ethnicity variables when that evidence was translated into practice-were neither clearly defined nor connected to mechanisms of health and disease. Such challenges are not unique to this area of the literature: Cross-national analyses of the evolution of census terminology, for instance, have demonstrated that racial and ethnic classifications are heterogeneous, complex, and inconsistently defined; and classifications are strongly influenced by variations within and across cultures over time. 27 Likewise, in a review of over a decade's worth of literature from the top 10 academic journals in general medicine, oncology, and surgery, it was found that 81 different classifications of race and ethnicity were used; and "these were often imprecise and open to interpretation." 28 Moreover, uses of race and ethnicity variables often lacked scientific rigor and reproducibility; less than 5% of articles provided a definition of race or ethnicity and just over 10% described how race and ethnicity data were classified. 28 he failure to connect race and ethnicity variables to mechanisms by which disparities occur, while also prevalent in the extant literature about health disparities, forestalls scientific and clinical advancement by de-emphasizing the identification and evaluation of interventions that can reduce disparities.

documents.title: Nonrandom Missingness in Child Race and Ethnicity Records and the US Federal Data Standards: Pooled Analysis of Community-Based Child Health Studies
documents.snippet:
Retrospectively harmonizing survey data across 8 community-based child health studies revealed new insights into how past, current, and new federal data standards can influence the representation of marginalized racial and ethnic populations in public health research, policy, and practice. We observed significant changes in the racial and ethnic composition of our sample after reallocating parent-provided written and categorical responses on child race or ethnicity surveys into federally defined categories. Our findings add to the existing literature underscoring how specific components of survey research design disproportionately threaten the quality, completeness, and internal validity of social determinants of health data for minoritized racial populations [41]. The inconsistencies in survey design and methodology we identified may reinforce racial health disparities at the population level through racial group misclassification, nonresponse bias, and the obscuring of diversity through the aggregate multiracial category, thereby warranting further hypothesis testing [42]. Continuing to overlook these survey research elements-open-ended responses, the other race category, and multiracial populations-may hinder racial equity by contributing to an evidence base that lacks validity and reliability for racial and ethnic groups that are exposed to multiple forms of discrimination. The trends we observed between written and categorical responses underscore that race and ethnicity are context-specific, fluid, and dynamic social constructs, which researchers and policymakers should carefully consider during data collection, analysis, and dissemination [5]. 

Currently, public health researchers and surveillance methods may not adequately account for the confusion that can result from inconsistent or conflated terminology, government standards, and societal norms around race and ethnicity. In addition, internalized racism may lead many immigrants and members of marginalized racial groups to reject or not identify with federal racial or ethnic categories. For example, all surveys in our study enumerated the single combined Black or African American categorical response option; however, many children were reallocated into this category because their parents checked other race and provided written data, such as "Haitian," "Cape Verdean," or "Black." Documented differences in group consciousness between foreign and US-born Black individuals could partially explain this discrepancy [43].

Lastly, we hypothesize that there will be no differences in measurement error of height by race and ethnicity: irrespective of race and ethnicity, women with higher (college/some college) vs. lower (≤high school) educational attainment will be less likely to misreport height.

Title: A Quasi-Experiment comparing the health of unhoused people who have and have not experienced an eviction in King County, WA
Snippet: Race and ethnicity were collected using two separate survey items: one asking about racial identity and another asking whether the respondent identified as Hispanic or Latino. In reviewing the data, we observed a nontrivial pattern of missingness in these responses. Some respondents skipped multiple demographic items, consistent with typical nonresponse behavior Tourangeau et al. [2014]. However, a cluster of respondents answered other demographic and sensitive questions (e.g., substance use, mental health) but either skipped or selected "Do not know" for race and/or ethnicity. We interpret this second pattern as reflecting question design effects: specifically, the absence of "Hispanic" as a race option may have confused respondents who primarily identify as Hispanic or Latino Passel [2024]. 

Our recoding approach reflects a conceptual distinction between three types of responses: (1) affirmative identification, (2) explicit uncertainty ("Do not know"), and (3) nonresponse ("Choose not to answer" or skip). We treat "Do not know" not as missing, but as a meaningful non-affirmative response, indicating that the respondent engaged with the question but did not (or could not) classify themselves using the available categories. Studies also showed that excluding "Do not know" responses poses a threat to validity Waters et al. [2022], Denman et al. [2018]. In contrast, skipped or refused items were coded as missing and excluded from analysis. 

To construct a combined race/ethnicity variable, we followed the recent updates in the U.S. Census questionnaire Office of Management and Budget [2024] while adapting for our survey structure. Respondents who identified as Hispanic or Latino were categorized as "Hispanic (any race)," regardless of their race response. Non-Hispanic respondents who reported a valid race were classified accordingly. If race was answered as "Do not know" or left blank, but ethnicity was clearly non-Hispanic, the respondent was assigned to "Non-Hispanic -Race not reported." Finally, respondents who provided neither a race nor an ethnicity response were coded as missing on the combined variable and excluded from analyses. 

This strategy balances alignment with federal standards, conceptual clarity around types of nonresponse, and pragmatic concerns around retaining analytical sample size.

Title: Triangulating Differential Nonresponse by Race in a Telephone Survey
Snippet: Introduction In 1994, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services mandated sufficient inclusion of racial and ethnic minorities in all federally funded research. This mandate requires researchers to monitor study samples for research participation and differential survey nonresponse. This study illustrates methods to assess differential survey nonresponse when population race data are incomplete, which is often the case when studies are conducted among members of health plans. Methods We collected data as part of the PRISM (Personally Relevant Information about Screening Mammography) study, a trial funded by the National Institutes of Health to increase rates of annual mammography adherence. We used two methods to estimate racial distribution of the PRISM study population. The first method, called E-Tech, estimated race of the sample frame by using individuals' names and zip codes. In the second method, we conducted interviews with a subsample of PRISM study refusals. We validated both estimation methods through comparisons with self-reported race. We used race information generated by E-Tech, interviewer estimates, and self-report to assess differential nonresponse in the PRISM study. Results The E-Tech method had moderate sensitivity (48%) in estimating race of black participants but higher specificity (97%) and positive predictive value (71%). The interviewer-estimation method had high sensitivity (100%), high specificity (95%), and moderate positive predictive value (80%). Black women were less likely than white women to be reached for study participation. Conclusion There was slight differential nonresponse by race in the PRISM study. Techniques described here may be useful for assessing differential nonresponse in samples with incomplete data on race.

Title: Tailored Explanation: A Strategy to Minimize Nonresponse in Demographic Items Among Low-income Racial and Ethnic Minorities
Snippet: Incomplete data in surveys is a major concern for researchers. Data incompleteness can be associated with undercoverage, unit nonresponse, and/ or item nonresponse (Groves et al. 2009). This paper focuses on item nonresponse specifically to demographic items including income, race, gender, and age. Item nonresponse occurs when the respondents in the selected sample provide some, but not all, of the requested information (Groves et al. 2009). Item nonresponse can lead to bias and measurement errors. Thus, it is essential to reduce item nonresponse.

Title: Hurdles to inference: The demographic correlates of survey breakoff and shirking
Snippet: Survey research uses total survey error to map out the possible threats that lead to biased inferences and creates a framework for researchers to holistically think about maximizing data quality while balancing the financial and time constraints of designing surveys, obtaining samples, and analyzing responses (Groves et al. 2009;Weisberg 2005). This framework outlines errors to include a sampling error (an error from estimating population characteristics from a sample), coverage error (an error when members of the population are excluded from the sample), measurement error (an error where the observed value differs from the "true" value), nonresponse error (when respondents in the sample do not respond or incompleteness of responses in sample), and postsurvey error (an error produced through data editing, weighting, and encoding). Within this framework, we focus on nonresponse errors that are produced through incompleteness or inattentiveness. The latter creates a potentially larger concern given some response seem "complete" but lack being quality responses. The error is exacerbated when there are systematic differences in the types of respondents who use different types of nonresponse behaviors. Importantly, this is an error that can manifest within high-quality, representative samples, using nonbiased question construction.

There is some extant research on demographic correlates in survey nonresponse. Past articles have observed correlations between race and gender and the likelihood of an individual breaking off during a survey (Peytchev 2009;Steinbrecher, Roßmann, and Blumenstiel 2015). If breakoff were unrelated to individual characteristics it presents a problem in terms of costs and efficiency, but the threat to validity would be minimal. However, if certain types of people are more likely to break off their participation, we must account for this risk.

As a result, the range of ethnic categories of interviewers and respondents considered in previous research has been extremely limited, rooted in the American experience of inter-race relations and, to a lesser extent, relations between Hispanics and non-Hispanics. Work has only recently begun to expand to other contexts where survey enumerators' outwardly observable ethnic characteristics are salient due to a history of conflict or competition between descent-based groupings.

documents.title: Triangulating Differential Nonresponse by Race in a Telephone Survey
documents.snippet: Introduction In 1994, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services mandated sufficient inclusion of racial and ethnic minorities in all federally funded research. This mandate requires researchers to monitor study samples for research participation and differential survey nonresponse. This study illustrates methods to assess differential survey nonresponse when population race data are incomplete, which is often the case when studies are conducted among members of health plans. Methods We collected data as part of the PRISM (Personally Relevant Information about Screening Mammography) study, a trial funded by the National Institutes of Health to increase rates of annual mammography adherence. We used two methods to estimate racial distribution of the PRISM study population. The first method, called E-Tech, estimated race of the sample frame by using individuals' names and zip codes. In the second method, we conducted interviews with a subsample of PRISM study refusals. We validated both estimation methods through comparisons with self-reported race. We used race information generated by E-Tech, interviewer estimates, and self-report to assess differential nonresponse in the PRISM study. Results The E-Tech method had moderate sensitivity (48%) in estimating race of black participants but higher specificity (97%) and positive predictive value (71%). The interviewer-estimation method had high sensitivity (100%), high specificity (95%), and moderate positive predictive value (80%). Black women were less likely than white women to be reached for study participation. Conclusion There was slight differential nonresponse by race in the PRISM study. Techniques described here may be useful for assessing differential nonresponse in samples with incomplete data on race.

documents.title: Tailored Explanation: A Strategy to Minimize Nonresponse in Demographic Items Among Low-income Racial and Ethnic Minorities
documents.snippet: Incomplete data in surveys is a major concern for researchers. Data incompleteness can be associated with undercoverage, unit nonresponse, and/ or item nonresponse (Groves et al. 2009). This paper focuses on item nonresponse specifically to demographic items including income, race, gender, and age. Item nonresponse occurs when the respondents in the selected sample provide some, but not all, of the requested information (Groves et al. 2009). Item nonresponse can lead to bias and measurement errors. Thus, it is essential to reduce item nonresponse.

documents.title: Hurdles to inference: The demographic correlates of survey breakoff and shirking
documents.snippet:
Survey research uses total survey error to map out the possible threats that lead to biased inferences and creates a framework for researchers to holistically think about maximizing data quality while balancing the financial and time constraints of designing surveys, obtaining samples, and analyzing responses (Groves et al. 2009;Weisberg 2005). This framework outlines errors to include a sampling error (an error from estimating population characteristics from a sample), coverage error (an error when members of the population are excluded from the sample), measurement error (an error where the observed value differs from the "true" value), nonresponse error (when respondents in the sample do not respond or incompleteness of responses in sample), and postsurvey error (an error produced through data editing, weighting, and encoding). Within this framework, we focus on nonresponse errors that are produced through incompleteness or inattentiveness. The latter creates a potentially larger concern given some response seem "complete" but lack being quality responses. The error is exacerbated when there are systematic differences in the types of respondents who use different types of nonresponse behaviors. Importantly, this is an error that can manifest within high-quality, representative samples, using nonbiased question construction.

There is some extant research on demographic correlates in survey nonresponse. Past articles have observed correlations between race and gender and the likelihood of an individual breaking off during a survey (Peytchev 2009;Steinbrecher, Roßmann, and Blumenstiel 2015). Unsurprisingly, there is evidence that respondent interest plays a large role in the propensity to break off from a survey (Galesic 2006;Groves, Presser, and Dipko 2004;Krosnick 1991), with cognitive ability, age, and education also quite influential (Conrad, Schober, and Dijkstra 2008;Knauper 1999). Obviously, these differences in propensity to break off have major substantive implications. If breakoff were unrelated to individual characteristics it presents a problem in terms of costs and efficiency, but the threat to validity would be minimal. However, if certain types of people are more likely to break off their participation, we must account for this risk.
